claim: Deployment of covert attention to a spatial location can cause large decreases in low-frequency correlated variability among neurons in macaque area V4 whose receptive-fields lie at the attended location.
source: Deployment of covert attention to a spatial location can cause large decreases in low-frequency correlated variability among neurons in macaque area V4 whose receptive-fields lie at the attended location.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in the field.

claim: The reduction in correlated variability accounts for a substantial fraction of the attention-mediated improvement in sensory processing.
source: It has been estimated that this reduction accounts for a substantial fraction of the attention-mediated improvement in sensory processing.
evidence: This claim is based on estimates from prior theoretical work, as indicated by the phrase 'it has been estimated'.

claim: Low-frequency optical stimulation of neurons in V4 elevates correlations among pairs of neurons.
source: We find that low-frequency optical stimulation of neurons in V4 elevates correlations among pairs of neurons and impairs the animal's ability to make fine sensory discriminations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 3A showing increased spike-count correlations.

claim: Low-frequency optical stimulation of neurons in V4 impairs the animal's ability to make fine sensory discriminations.
source: We find that low-frequency optical stimulation of neurons in V4 elevates correlations among pairs of neurons and impairs the animal's ability to make fine sensory discriminations.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing increased discrimination thresholds during low-frequency stimulation (Figure 2C).

claim: Stimulation at higher frequencies does not impair performance, despite comparable modulation of neuronal responses.
source: Stimulation at higher frequencies does not impair performance, despite comparable modulation of neuronal responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral and physiological data comparing high-frequency and low-frequency stimulation conditions (Figures 2E, 3B, 4).

claim: Neurons exhibit responses that are highly variable.
source: Neurons exhibit responses that are highly variable (Shadlen and Newsome, 1998), with nearby neurons in the cortex exhibiting correlated variability in their spiking output (Cohen and Kohn, 2011; Smith and Kohn, 2008; Smith and Sommer, 2013; Zohary et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Nearby neurons in the cortex exhibit correlated variability in their spiking output.
source: Neurons exhibit responses that are highly variable (Shadlen and Newsome, 1998), with nearby neurons in the cortex exhibiting correlated variability in their spiking output (Cohen and Kohn, 2011; Smith and Kohn, 2008; Smith and Sommer, 2013; Zohary et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Even weak correlations substantially reduce the information coding capacity of a population.
source: It has been estimated on theoretical grounds that even weak correlations substantially reduce the information coding capacity of a population (Zohary et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical estimates from cited prior work.

claim: Spatial attention can reduce correlated variability among neurons in macaque visual area V4.
source: Spatial attention can reduce correlated variability (often referred to as noise correlations) among neurons in macaque visual area V4 (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009), an area that is strongly modulated by spatial attention (Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Area V4 is strongly modulated by spatial attention.
source: Spatial attention can reduce correlated variability (often referred to as noise correlations) among neurons in macaque visual area V4 (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009), an area that is strongly modulated by spatial attention (Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The reduction in correlated variability due to attention is restricted to low frequencies below 10 Hz.
source: Mitchell et al., 2009 found that this reduction is restricted to low frequencies below 10 Hz.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The reduction in correlated variability accounts for about 80% of the perceptual benefit due to attention.
source: These studies have estimated, on theoretical grounds, that the reduction in correlated variability accounts for a large fraction (about 80%) of the perceptual benefit due to attention.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical estimates from prior studies.

claim: Estimates of the perceptual benefit from reduced correlations rely on specific assumptions about the relationship between noise and signal correlations.
source: However, these estimates rely on specific assumptions about the relationship between noise and signal correlations, and thereby, on how population signals are read out in the brain (Abbott and Dayan, 1999; Averbeck et al., 2006; Moreno-Bote et al., 2014; Panzeri et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work discussing assumptions in decoding models.

claim: Correlated variability does not necessarily limit information when using heterogeneous tuning curves and optimal readout.
source: Theoretical studies using heterogeneous tuning curves and optimal readout have concluded that correlated variability does not necessarily limit information (Ecker et al., 2011; Shamir and Sompolinsky, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: A recent study found improved sensory discrimination when neurons in Area V4 were desynchronized.
source: Consistent with the interpretation that attention-dependent reductions in correlated variability improve perception, a recent study of the effects of naturally occurring fluctuations in neural correlations found improved sensory discrimination when neurons in Area V4 were desynchronized (Beaman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Correlations may be induced by fluctuations in attention.
source: However, other studies have posited that correlations themselves may be induced by fluctuations in attention (Goris et al., 2014), resulting in variation in response gain that is shared across neurons, and other experiments have shown that attention can, under some conditions, also increase correlated neural response variability (Ruff and Cohen, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Attention can, under some conditions, increase correlated neural response variability.
source: However, other studies have posited that correlations themselves may be induced by fluctuations in attention (Goris et al., 2014), resulting in variation in response gain that is shared across neurons, and other experiments have shown that attention can, under some conditions, also increase correlated neural response variability (Ruff and Cohen, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The causal role of correlated variability in perception has not been tested prior to this study.
source: Importantly, all of these studies are correlative in nature. The causal role of correlated variability in perception has not been tested and thus the proposal that low-frequency correlated variability is detrimental for perception has remained purely hypothetical.
evidence: This claim is based on a review of prior literature and the identification of a gap in causal evidence.

claim: Attentional modulation of correlated variability is spatially selective.
source: We exploited the fact that attentional modulation of correlated variability is both spatially- and frequency selective: attention-dependent reductions in correlation are restricted to low frequencies (<10 Hz (Mitchell et al., 2009)).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Attentional modulation of correlated variability is frequency selective, with reductions restricted to low frequencies (<10 Hz).
source: We exploited the fact that attentional modulation of correlated variability is both spatially- and frequency selective: attention-dependent reductions in correlation are restricted to low frequencies (<10 Hz (Mitchell et al., 2009)).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The correlations that impair perception may have an inherent time scale, with low- but not high-frequency correlations impairing perception.
source: We reasoned that the correlations that impair perception may have an inherent time scale, with low- but not high-frequency correlations impairing perception.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on prior findings about frequency-selective attention effects.

claim: The artificial dura approach provides an optically clear window into the awake-behaving primate brain.
source: This approach provides an optically clear window into the awake-behaving primate brain and allows precise opto-electrophysiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the method and citations to prior work using this approach.

claim: A lenti-viral construct was injected to preferentially drive expression of the depolarizing opsin C1V1 in excitatory neurons.
source: We injected a lenti-viral construct (lenti-CaMKIIa-C1V1E162T-ts-EYFP) to preferentially drive expression of the depolarizing opsin C1V1 in excitatory neurons (Yizhar et al., 2011) in a restricted portion (200-300 µm diameter) of dorsal V4 of two macaque monkeys (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods and citation to prior work on the opsin.

claim: There was similar orientation tuning among neurons within each injection site.
source: Despite some heterogeneity in orientation tuning width at each injection site, overall there was similar tuning among neurons within a site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Impaired performance and slower reaction times were observed for foil trials, indicating that the monkey was using the spatial cue.
source: Impaired performance (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, left panel, square symbol) and slower reaction times (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, right panel, square symbol) were observed for the foil trials, indicating that the monkey was indeed using the spatial cue in performing the task.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Low-frequency optical stimulation modulates the timing of the neural response but does not alter the overall magnitude of the population response.
source: We find that low-frequency optical stimulation modulates the timing of the neural response (Figure 4D) but does not alter the overall magnitude of the population response (Figure 4A, B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by physiological data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The induced correlations were at a level comparable in strength to that observed when attention was directed away from the RF location in the baseline condition.
source: The induced correlations were at a level comparable in strength to that observed when attention was directed away from the RF location in the baseline condition (Figure 3A, left panel; blue versus white bar).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Unit activity shows phase locking to optical stimulation.
source: Rather, unit activity shows phase locking to optical stimulation (Figure 4D,E; pre-stimulus period).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: The peak of the phase-lock distribution for the stimulus presentation period occurs earlier than for the pre-stimulus period because neurons are depolarized by the visual stimulus.
source: This would be expected, as the neurons are depolarized by the visual stimulus and hence more easily pushed to spiking threshold by optogenetic depolarization, as compared to when no stimulus is present.
evidence: This is an inference based on known neurophysiology and the observed data.

claim: Low-frequency stimulation impairs the monkey's ability to detect fine orientation changes only at the opsin location.
source: Behaviorally, we find that low-frequency stimulation impairs the monkey's ability to detect fine orientation changes, and does so only at the opsin location, as indicated by impairment in the attend-in condition (Figure 2B, upper panel; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), not in the attend-away condition (Figure 2B, lower panel), in which the monkey discriminated orientation at the contralateral location.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In a large fraction of individual behavioral sessions, both changes in threshold and slope were significant.
source: In a large fraction of individual behavioral sessions (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B), both the changes in threshold and slope were significant (20/42 sessions).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of individual session data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B.

claim: There was no significant change in PDMI on trials when the monkey was cued to detect the target at the unstimulated location.
source: The impairment due to optical stimulation is location specific: there was no significant change in PDMI on trials when the monkey was cued to detect the target at the unstimulated location (attend-away condition, Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: High-frequency stimulation produces no significant change in PDMI despite a significant increase in high-frequency spike-count correlations.
source: Importantly, the impairment is also frequency specific. When we stimulate the neurons with 20Hz sinusoidally modulated low-power laser stimulation ('high-frequency stimulation' condition), we observed no significant change in PDMI (Figure 2E), despite a significant increase in high-frequency spike-count correlations (Figure 3B) and phase locking comparable to the low-frequency stimulation condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral and physiological data shown in Figures 2E, 3B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is no significant change in mean firing rates with the high-frequency stimulation condition.
source: As in the low-frequency stimulation condition, we find no significant changes in mean firing rates with the high-frequency stimulation condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no phase preference for target stimulus onset with respect to laser stimulation.
source: To verify that such phase alignment did not nonetheless occur by chance, we measured the phase of target stimulus onset for both low- and high-frequency stimulation and found no phase preference (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Orientation tuning curves were not significantly altered by the laser at either frequency.
source: We find that orientation tuning curves were not significantly altered by the laser at either frequency (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), at least in the range of orientations used in the experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: There is no evidence that laser stimulation caused frequency-dependent adaptation that would reduce responses to visual stimuli.
source: To test this, we measured the firing rates evoked by the first four non-target stimulus flashes, on no-laser, low-frequency laser and high-frequency laser trials, in the 'attend in' condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 5). Though the first stimulus in the sequence evoked a stronger response than the subsequent stimuli (reflecting a form of visual stimulus-driven adaptation), we find no evidence that the addition of the laser at either frequency caused a change in mean firing rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: V4 has patchy organization for orientation tuning, so simultaneously recorded neurons tended to prefer similar orientations.
source: V4 has patchy organization for orientation tuning, so simultaneously recorded neurons tended to prefer similar orientations (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and established knowledge about V4 organization.

claim: Where signal correlations are positive, positive noise correlations should reduce discriminability by increasing the overlap between neural responses evoked by discriminanda.
source: Under these conditions, where signal correlations are positive, positive noise correlations should reduce discriminability (Averbeck et al., 2006) by increasing the overlap between neural responses evoked by discriminanda.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical work cited and logical inference.

claim: Sessions in which low-frequency laser-induced correlations caused the strongest perceptual suppression all showed negative NDMIs.
source: In both analyses, the sessions in which low-frequency laser-induced correlations caused the strongest perceptual suppression all showed negative NDMIs.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the relationship between NDMI and PDMI shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Laser-induced reductions in discriminability at the neural level corresponded to increased perceptual thresholds.
source: In other words, laser-induced reductions in discriminability at the neural level corresponded to increased perceptual thresholds.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the correlation between NDMI and PDMI shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no significant correlation between NDMI and changes in the slope of the psychometric function.
source: There was no significant correlation between NDMI and changes in the slope of the psychometric function.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the relationship between NDMI and slope changes.

claim: NDMI calculated from hit trials had no correlation with threshold or slope changes.
source: NDMI calculated from hit trials had no correlation with threshold or slope changes.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of NDMI from hit trials.

claim: It is possible to induce coherent activity in a neuronal ensemble due to sub-threshold rhythmic stimulation.
source: To confirm whether it is possible to induce coherent activity in a neuronal ensemble due to sub-threshold rhythmic stimulation, we examined the consequences of such stimulation on a conductance-based model of excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Figure 6A; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Sub-threshold stimulation can induce coherent activity in the network at a desired frequency.
source: We find that it is indeed possible to induce coherent activity in the network at a desired frequency (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) and that this induction is robust to a wide range of network (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) and stimulation parameters (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6D and supplementary figures.

claim: The location specificity of the impairment suggests that the impairment is not due to a phosphene effect.
source: The location specificity of the impairment also suggests that the impairment is not due to a phosphene effect (Jazayeri et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial specificity of the behavioral effect and citation to prior work on phosphenes.

claim: If attention were drawn away from the unstimulated location by a phosphene, impaired performance would be expected in the attend-away condition.
source: If attention were drawn away from the unstimulated location by a phosphene we would expect impaired performance in the attend-away condition.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected if a phosphene were causing the effect.

claim: Stimulation at a non-opsin site does not cause changes in behavior.
source: We also verified that the impairment was not due to a thermal effect by stimulating a location in the chamber a few millimeters from the opsin site (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A) and not due to visual distractions caused by the laser light by stimulating outside the brain (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B). In both cases, we did not observe any changes in behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Stimulation outside the brain does not cause changes in behavior.
source: We also verified that the impairment was not due to a thermal effect by stimulating a location in the chamber a few millimeters from the opsin site (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A) and not due to visual distractions caused by the laser light by stimulating outside the brain (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B). In both cases, we did not observe any changes in behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: It is reasonable to assume that the opsin was strongly biased toward pyramidal neurons.
source: Thus, we do not have a measure of lenti/CAMKII selectivity in macaque V4. However, it is reasonable to assume that the opsin was strongly biased toward pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work showing selectivity in V1 and other brain areas.

claim: In a previous study in V1, lenti/CAMKII expressing C1V1/EYFP led to expression that was highly selective for excitatory neurons.
source: In that study, lenti/CAMKII expressing C1V1/EYFP led to expression that was highly selective for excitatory neurons (Figure 1B of Nassi et al., 2015): of 119 neurons imaged in five different fields of view, only 2 (1.7%) were double labeled for both EYFP and parvalbumin/calretinin/calbindin, indicating that expression was heavily biased toward excitatory neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CaMKII has been used in other macaque brain areas including perirhinal cortex, where it led to opsin expression primarily in excitatory neurons.
source: CaMKII has also been used in other macaque brain areas including perirhinal cortex (Tamura et al., 2017), where it also led to opsin expression primarily in excitatory neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The results establish the first causal link between correlated variability and perception.
source: Our results establish the first causal link between correlated variability and perception.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The optogenetic stimulation protocol induces correlations that might not be physiologically realistic.
source: The optogenetic stimulation protocol in our study, using sinusoidal modulation of laser irradiance, induces the kind of correlations in a local population of the cortex that might not be physiologically realistic.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: The study establishes the causal relevance of low-frequency correlated variability in perception.
source: It nevertheless establishes the causal relevance of low-frequency correlated variability in perception and supports the hypothesis that attention-dependent reductions in correlated variability enhance perception.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings.

claim: The correlations induced in the study included information-limiting correlations.
source: Recently, studies have theorized that only certain correlations – those that are indistinguishable from stimulus-induced correlations – are information limiting (Moreno-Bote et al., 2014). We speculate that the correlations induced in our study included such information-limiting correlations, resulting in the observed impairment.
evidence: This is speculation based on theoretical work and the observed results.

claim: The timescale of low-frequency correlations is consistent with inter-saccadic intervals (200–300 ms).
source: The timescale of these low-frequency correlations is consistent with inter-saccadic intervals (200–300 ms), which may be a relevant timeframe for gathering visual information (Yarbus et al., 1967).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the timescale of correlations to a known behavioral timescale, supported by citation.

claim: Decreases in correlated variability at the inter-saccadic timescale could be critical for perception.
source: Decreases in correlated variability at this timescale could therefore be critical for perception.
evidence: This is speculation based on the connection between correlation timescales and behavioral timescales.

claim: Human observers are better able to discriminate stimulus orientations near the cardinal than oblique orientations.
source: Psychophysical studies have found that human observers are better able to discriminate stimulus orientations near the cardinal than oblique orientations (Girshick et al., 2011; Heeley and Timney, 1988; Appelle, 1972; Orban et al., 1984; Campbell et al., 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior psychophysical research.

claim: Cardinal orientations are overrepresented in V1.
source: Electrophysiological and imaging studies in humans, monkeys, cats and ferrets have found that cardinal orientations are overrepresented in V1 (De Valois et al., 1982; Furmanski and Engel, 2000; Li et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2003; Chapman and Bonhoeffer, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological and imaging studies.
